lead: Reciprocity and symmetry are two properties you can test from the parameters alone, without opening the box. A reciprocal network transfers equally in both directions: a current into port 1 produces the same open-circuit voltage at port 2 as the same current into port 2 produces at port 1. A symmetric network looks the same from either port, so the two ports can be swapped without any change outside. Each property removes one independent parameter, and both simplify the input impedance and gain of a terminated two-port.
prereq: You need Z and Y parameters, h and g parameters, ABCD parameters, the conversion table and the reciprocity theorem from network theorems.

blocks.text: Drive port 1 with a current I with port 2 open: the voltage at port 2 is z₂₁I. Drive port 2 with the same I with port 1 open: the voltage at port 1 is z₁₂I. The reciprocity theorem says that in a linear network of R, L, C, coupled coils and ideal transformers the two responses are equal. So a reciprocal network has z₁₂ = z₂₁, and the conversion table turns this into a condition for every set:

blocks.text: The minus sign in the h test comes from the short-circuit measurement: h₂₁ = I₂/I₁ with port 2 shorted, and in a passive network the current flows out of terminal 2 into the short, against the entering arrow. Dependent sources usually break reciprocity; a transistor model is not reciprocal. A reciprocal two-port has three independent parameters.

sections.h3: Symmetry: the same from either port

blocks.text: A two-port is (electrically) symmetric when swapping ports 1 and 2 changes nothing at the terminals. The open-circuit input impedance then equals the open-circuit output impedance, z₁₁ = z₂₂. Through the table:

The h test follows from h₁₁ = Δz/z₂₂, h₂₂ = 1/z₂₂, h₁₂h₂₁ = −z₁₂z₂₁/z₂₂², which give Δh = z₁₁/z₂₂. The ABCD test follows from A = z₁₁/z₂₁ and D = z₂₂/z₂₁. A passive network that is symmetric and reciprocal is fixed by only two parameters, for example z₁₁ and z₁₂. A network drawn with mirror symmetry (a T with Z₁ = Z₂, a lattice) is always electrically symmetric, but a reciprocal network need not be symmetric: the T network of this unit has z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 4 Ω but z₁₁ = 6 Ω ≠ z₂₂ = 7 Ω.
Put a source of internal impedance Z<sub>S</sub> at port 1 and a load Z<sub>L</sub> at port 2. The load gives V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub>; substituting in the Z equations and eliminating I₂:
Zin = z₁₁ − z₁₂z₂₁/(z₂₂ + ZL) and, looking back into port 2, Zout = z₂₂ − z₁₂z₂₁/(z₁₁ + ZS).
Current gain I₂/I₁ = −z₂₁/(z₂₂ + ZL) and voltage gain V₂/V₁ = z₂₁ZL/(Δz + z₁₁ZL).

For a reciprocal network z₁₂z₂₁ = z₁₂², and for a symmetric one Z<sub>in</sub> and Z<sub>out</sub> have the same form. The same quantities in ABCD form are Z<sub>in</sub> = (AZ<sub>L</sub> + B)/(CZ<sub>L</sub> + D) and Z<sub>out</sub> = (DZ<sub>S</sub> + B)/(CZ<sub>S</sub> + A); note that A and D swap when you look in from the other end.

figure.caption: The reciprocity test on the T network: 1 A into either port gives 4 V at the other, open port, so z₁₂ = z₂₁. The open-circuit impedances 6 Ω and 7 Ω differ, so the network is reciprocal but not symmetric.

examples.question: For the T network with z₁₁ = 6 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 4 Ω, z₂₂ = 7 Ω: (a) test reciprocity and symmetry in Z, h and ABCD form; (b) with a 3 Ω load, find Z<sub>in</sub>, the current gain and the voltage gain; (c) with a 2 Ω source resistance, find Z<sub>out</sub>.
steps: Z form: z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 4 Ω, so reciprocal; z₁₁ = 6 Ω ≠ z₂₂ = 7 Ω, so not symmetric.
h form (h₁₂ = 4/7, h₂₁ = −4/7, h₁₁ = 26/7 Ω, h₂₂ = 1/7 S): h₁₂ = −h₂₁ ✓ reciprocal; Δh = 26/49 + 16/49 = 42/49 = 0.857 ≠ 1, not symmetric. ABCD form: AD − BC = 1 ✓; A = 1.5 ≠ D = 1.75.
Current gain I₂/I₁ = −4/(7 + 3) = −0.4: the load takes 0.4 of the input current, flowing out of terminal 2.
Voltage gain V₂/V₁ = z₂₁Z<sub>L</sub>/(Δz + z₁₁Z<sub>L</sub>) = 4 × 3/(26 + 18) = 12/44 = 0.2727. Check: V₂/V₁ = (−I₂Z<sub>L</sub>)/(I₁Z<sub>in</sub>) = 0.4 × 3/4.4 = 0.2727 ✓.
examples.answer: Reciprocal but not symmetric in every form; Z<sub>in</sub> = 4.4 Ω, I₂/I₁ = −0.4, V₂/V₁ = 0.2727 with the 3 Ω load; Z<sub>out</sub> = 5 Ω with the 2 Ω source.

examples.question: The shunt arm of the same T network gets a current-controlled voltage source 2I₁ (2 Ω × I₁) in series with its 4 Ω resistor, adding to the voltage across that arm. Find the Z parameters and test reciprocity.
steps: Centre-node voltage: the arm carries I₁ + I₂, so V<sub>c</sub> = 4(I₁ + I₂) + 2I₁ = 6I₁ + 4I₂.
V₁ = 2I₁ + V<sub>c</sub> = 8I₁ + 4I₂, so z₁₁ = 8 Ω and z₁₂ = 4 Ω.
V₂ = 3I₂ + V<sub>c</sub> = 6I₁ + 7I₂, so z₂₁ = 6 Ω and z₂₂ = 7 Ω.
z₁₂ = 4 Ω ≠ z₂₁ = 6 Ω: not reciprocal. In ABCD form AD − BC = z₁₂/z₂₁ = 4/6 = 0.667 ≠ 1, and in h form h₁₂ = 4/7 = 0.571 while −h₂₁ = 6/7 = 0.857.
z₁₁ = 8 Ω ≠ z₂₂ = 7 Ω: not symmetric either.
examples.answer: z₁₁ = 8 Ω, z₁₂ = 4 Ω, z₂₁ = 6 Ω, z₂₂ = 7 Ω; the dependent source makes the network non-reciprocal (AD − BC = 0.667).

traps: Reciprocity is not symmetry. The T network is reciprocal (z₁₂ = z₂₁) but not symmetric (6 Ω ≠ 7 Ω).
In h and g parameters reciprocity carries a minus sign: h₁₂ = −h₂₁. Writing h₁₂ = h₂₁ fails every passive network.
AD − BC = 1 is the reciprocity test; A = D is the symmetry test. Swapping them is a common lost mark.
Symmetry in h form is Δh = 1, not Δh = 0 and not h₁₁ = h₂₂ (they do not even have the same unit).
Z<sub>in</sub> uses z₂₂ + Z<sub>L</sub> in the denominator and Z<sub>out</sub> uses z₁₁ + Z<sub>S</sub>. In ABCD form A and D swap places between Z<sub>in</sub> and Z<sub>out</sub>.

quiz.q: State the reciprocity condition in Z, Y, h and ABCD parameters.
quiz.a: z₁₂ = z₂₁; y₁₂ = y₂₁; h₁₂ = −h₂₁; AD − BC = 1.

quiz.q: State the symmetry condition in Z, Y, h and ABCD parameters.
quiz.a: z₁₁ = z₂₂; y₁₁ = y₂₂; Δh = 1; A = D.

quiz.q: Starting from z₁₂ = z₂₁, show that AD − BC = 1.
quiz.a: A = z₁₁/z₂₁, B = Δz/z₂₁, C = 1/z₂₁, D = z₂₂/z₂₁. AD − BC = (z₁₁z₂₂ − Δz)/z₂₁² = z₁₂z₂₁/z₂₁² = z₁₂/z₂₁, which is 1 when z₁₂ = z₂₁.

quiz.q: A two-port has z₁₁ = 5 Ω, z₂₂ = 8 Ω and z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 2 Ω. Is it reciprocal? Symmetric?
quiz.a: Reciprocal, since z₁₂ = z₂₁; not symmetric, since 5 Ω ≠ 8 Ω.

quiz.q: For z₁₁ = 10 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 6 Ω, z₂₂ = 15 Ω and Z<sub>L</sub> = 5 Ω, find Z<sub>in</sub>.
For the same network with Z<sub>S</sub> = 4 Ω, find Z<sub>out</sub>.
A symmetric T network has Z₁ = Z₂ = 5 Ω and Z₃ = 10 Ω. Show that it passes both tests in ABCD form.
quiz.a: z₁₁ = z₂₂ = 15 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 10 Ω, Δz = 225 − 100 = 125 Ω². A = 15/10 = 1.5, B = 12.5 Ω, C = 0.1 S, D = 1.5. A = D (symmetric) and AD − BC = 2.25 − 1.25 = 1 (reciprocal).

beyond: Not for the exam. Non-reciprocal parts are useful: isolators and circulators use magnetised ferrites to pass microwaves one way only and protect transmitters from reflected power. In S parameters, reciprocity is S₁₂ = S₂₁. Antenna engineers rely on reciprocity to measure an antenna's receiving pattern by transmitting. Search for “ferrite isolator” and “antenna reciprocity”.
